description: We are Astrix, a team of students from Zhytomyr Polytechnic State University taking on the challenge of building software to monitor astronaut health during space missions. We combine [software development, data analysis and cybersecurity] to build a reliable and secure solution.
summary:
Astro-health is an offline-first health monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions. On Moon and Mars missions, crews cannot count on instant help from Earth, yet five spaceflight hazards affect their bodies at the same time. Sidus lets an astronaut log 16 health metrics, from heart rate, sleep and glucose to bone markers, mood and radiation dose, in under a minute.

Every profile starts with a baseline measured on Earth, so results are compared with the astronaut’s own norm and with the chosen environment (Earth, Moon, Mars, orbit, open space). A rule-based engine, whose diagnostic core is written in C, produces “Suspected…” findings with plain-language explanations. An anatomy map lights up body zones in grey, yellow or red, so the crew sees the status at a glance.

What is new: a built-in sensorimotor reaction game, workout reminders with a training calendar, a full time-stamped history of measurements and findings, and a warning when a profile has not been updated for 24 hours. The interface is bilingual (English/Ukrainian).
details:
Spaceflight changes the body: muscles weaken, bones lose density, blood moves differently, vision can blur, radiation accumulates. The catch is that every body reacts in its own way, and a “population average” often stays silent exactly when your personal numbers are already off.

Crew Health Monitor solves this. The astronaut records a personal baseline once on Earth. From then on, the app compares every new reading against it and speaks up early: “Suspected…”. Not just numbers, but a clear explanation of what it could mean and what to do.

A living body map. An anatomical figure where problem zones light up yellow (caution) or red (critical). One glance instead of a 25-row table.
Diagnosis that knows where you are. Earth, Mars, Moon, deep space or orbit: gravity, expected radiation dose and thresholds all adapt.
A rule engine written in C. Fast and predictable, while Python handles data and interface.
A complete history. A calendar keeps every entry and every diagnosis with its exact time.
Protocol-based workout reminders, a freshness check (a “!” after 24 hours) and CSV export for the flight surgeon.
A coordination game. Instead of a dull questionnaire, the astronaut chases a moving spaceship with the cursor; the app scores it as a percentage and charts progress over time.
Two languages, English and Ukrainian, one click apart.

Why it matters
Far from Earth, communication is slow and the doctor is not in the next room. The app runs entirely locally, with no cloud and no internet, and gives the crew an early signal while a problem is still small. For long missions to Mars and the Moon, this is the kind of tool that is missing.

An honest note: this is a study project, not a medical device. The thresholds are screening values that a flight surgeon must review, so the app flags suspicions and a professional makes the diagnosis.

Technology
Python (Pandas, NumPy, Statistics), Streamlit, SQLite, and C connected through ctypes. The only JavaScript is the browser side of the mini-game, which just draws the ship while Python calculates the score. The team worked as four roles (data engineer, two backend developers, frontend developer), so the code is organised into files by owner.

Creativity
We combined diagnostics, illustrated anatomy and a game in one interface that even a tired astronaut can read at a glance. Instead of “here is your pulse”, we say “here is what changed compared with you”.

What we considered
Honest wording (“Suspected…”), robustness to missing data, privacy (everything stays local), accessibility (labels and tooltips, not colour alone), simplicity for a user under load, and automated tests that check every text is translated into both languages.
dataRefs: Factors and threshold: Accumulated radiation dose reaching 100% of the limit (600 mSv over a career) + exceeding the radiation dose rate.
Factors and threshold: A reduction in sleep by >25–30% from the 8-hour norm (< 6 hours/day) + a slowing of reaction time by >15–20% (or lapses > 500 ms).
Factors and threshold: Fasting glucose elevated by >25–40% above the normal range of 4.5–5.5 mmol/L ($\ge 7.0$ mmol/L) + Cortisol elevated by >30%.
Factors and threshold: A decrease in muscle thickness of >10–16% + a decrease in 1RM (strength metric) of >15–20%.
Factors and threshold: Vision decline (0 / hyperopic shift $\ge +0.50$ D) + Increase in systolic blood pressure by >10–15%
Factors and threshold: Systolic pressure elevation of >15–20% above the norm of 120 mmHg ($\ge 140$ mmHg) + Diastolic pressure elevation of >12–15% ($\ge 90$ mmHg).
Factors and threshold: Body weight decrease of >3–5% + Heart rate increase of >15–20% (or $\ge +30$ bpm upon change of position).
